### Ribo-seq

Ribo-seq was performed as previously described with some modifications (McGlincy and Ingolia, 2017). MV4;11 cells treated for 48 hr with either 0.1% DMSO, 2 µM C6, or 100 nM C16 were washed with ice-cold PBS and lysed in 400 µL Lysis Buffer (20 mM Tris, pH 7.4; 150 mM NaCl; 15 mM MgCl2; 1 mM DTT; 100 µg/mL cycloheximide; 1% Triton X-100; 25 U/mL Turbo DNase I) by incubation on ice for 10 min followed by homogenization by syringe. Lysates were cleared by centrifugation at 4°C, and RNA quantified by Qubit RNA HS Assay (Invitrogen) following the manufacturer’s instructions. 30 µg RNA was diluted in 200 µL Polysome Buffer (20 mM Tris, pH 7.4; 150 mM NaCl; 5 mM MgCl2; 1 mM DTT; 100 µg/mL cycloheximide) and incubated with 15 U RNase I (Lucigen) for 45 min while rotating at RT. RNA digestion was quenched with 10 µL SUPERaseIn RNase Inhibitor (Invitrogen) and samples transferred to 13 mm × 51 mm ultracentrifuge tubes (Beckman-Coulter), underlaid with 900 µL 1 M sucrose in polysome buffer supplemented with 20 U/mL SUPERaseIn RNase Inhibitor, and centrifuged at 540,628 × g 1 hr at 4°C. Ribosome pellets were suspended in TRIzol Reagent (Invitrogen), and RNA extracted from ribosome pellets by Direct-zol RNA MiniPrep Kit (Zymo Research). RNA and carrier glycogen were precipitated by adding 1.5 volumes 100% isopropanol supplemented with 0.12 M NaOAc, pH 5.5, followed by incubation on dry ice for 30 min and centrifugation at 16,800 × g for 30 min at 4°C. RNA was resuspended in 5 µL 10 mM Tris, pH 8.0, and 1× Denaturing Sample Loading Buffer (98% formamide; 10 mM EDTA; 300 µg/mL bromophenol blue) and subjected to electrophoresis on 15% polyacrylamide TBE-Urea gels (Invitrogen). Gels were stained briefly with 1× SYBR Gold (Invitrogen), 17–34 nucleotide fragments excised, and RNA fragments extracted by mechanical disruption, suspension in 500 µL RNA Gel Extraction Buffer (300 mM NaOAc, pH 5.5; 1 mM EDTA; 0.25% SDS), freezing on dry ice for 30 min, and rotating overnight at RT. Polyacrylamide was removed by centrifugation through Costar Spin-X columns (Corning) and RNA precipitated with isopropanol as described above. RNA was dephosphorylated by incubation with 5 U T4 Polynucleotide Kinase in 1× T4 PNK Buffer (New England BioLabs) supplemented with SUPERaseIn RNase Inhibitor for 1 hr at 37°C and ligated to bar-coded linkers (NI-810: /5Phos/NNNNNATCGTAGATCGGAAGAGCACACGTCTGAA/3ddC/; NI-811: /5Phos/NNNNNAGCTAAGATCGGAAGAGCACACGTCTGAA/3ddC/; NI-812: /5Phos/NNNNNCGTAAAGATCGGAAGAGCACACGTCTGAA/3ddC/) pre-adenylated with 100 U of T4 RNA Ligase 2, truncated K227Q, in 1X T4 RNA Ligase Buffer (New England BioLabs) supplemented with 35% w/v PEG-8000 and incubated at 37°C for 3 hr. Ligation was verified by electrophoresis, samples combined, and linker-ligated RNA precipitated with isopropanol as described above. Ribosomal RNA was depleted from samples using the RiboCop rRNA Depletion Kit (Lexogen) and RNA precipitated with isopropanol as described above. Linker-ligated RNA was reverse transcribed with 200 U SuperScript III in 1× First Strand Buffer (Invitrogen), dNTPs, DTT, 10 U SUPERaseIn RNase Inhibitor and primer NI-802 (/5Phos/NNAGATCGGAAGAGCGTCGTGTAGGGAAAGAG/iSp18/GTGACTGGAGTTCAGACGTGTGCTC). RNA template was hydrolyzed for 15 min at 98°C in the presence of 0.1 M NaOH and cDNA precipitated with isopropanol as described previously. Reverse-transcribed DNA was subjected to electrophoresis on 15% polyacrylamide Novex TBE-Urea gels (Invitrogen) and the 105-nucleotide reverse-transcription product excised from polyacrylamide as described above, except with DNA Gel Extraction Buffer (300 mM NaCl; 10 mM Tris, pH 8.0; 1 mM EDTA). cDNA was circularized with 100 U CircLigase ssDNA Ligase (Lucigen) in the presence of 1× CircLigase Buffer, ATP, and MnCl2 at 60°C for 1 hr followed by 80°C for 10 min. Circularized cDNA was quantified by qPCR, amplified using Phusion Polymerase (New England BioLabs) with unique dual-indexed primers (UDI0050_i5: AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACACGCTCCGACACACTCTTTCCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT; UDI0050_i7: CAAGCAGAAGACGGCATACGAGATTAGAGCGCGTGACTGGAGTTCAGACGTGT; UDI0051_i5: AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACACATACCAAGACACTCTTTCCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT; UDI0051_i7: CAAGCAGAAGACGGCATACGAGATAACCTGTTGTGACTGGAGTTCAGACGTGT; UDI0052_i5: AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACACGCGTTGGAACACTCTTTCCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT; UDI0052_i7: CAAGCAGAAGACGGCATACGAGATGGTTCACCGTGACTGGAGTTCAGACGTGT), amplicons subjected to electrophoresis on 8% polyacrylamide Novex gels (Invitrogen), and products >160 bp excised as described. Libraries were submitted to VANTAGE (Vanderbilt Technologies for Advanced Genomics) for sequencing on a NovaSeq 6000.

### Ribo-seq data analysis

Adapters were trimmed from reads using cutadapt (Martin, 2011), and UMIs removed from reads and attached to read IDs using UMI-tools (Smith et al., 2017). Reads were demultiplexed using sabre and aligned against ribosomal RNA using bowtie2 (Langmead and Salzberg, 2012). Reads not mapping to rRNA were mapped to the hg19 transcriptome using STAR (Dobin et al., 2013) and deduplicated using UMI-tools (Smith et al., 2017). Count tables for reads mapping to central ORFs were generated using the coverage command from bedtools (Quinlan and Hall, 2010). After batch removal, Ribo-seq read counts were normalized to mRNA read counts using Xtail (Xiao et al., 2016) to calculate translation efficiencies and statistics. FDR values were calculated using the Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel test (CMH). Genes with significantly altered translation efficiencies were those with FDR < 0.05 and absolute log2FC > 0.25. Identification of optimal RPF P-site offsets, RPF triplet periodicity, and RPF localization to CDS and UTR regions was performed with the R package riboWaltz (Lauria et al., 2018).

### RNA-seq

For RNA-seq performed in parallel with Ribo-seq, RNA was isolated by Direct-zol RNA MiniPrep Kit (Zymo Research) from 100 µL of cell lysates after homogenization by syringe and clearing by centrifugation. For combination WINi/BETi treatment, MV4;11 cells were treated for 48 hr with either 0.2% DMSO, 100 nM C16, 2.5 nM mivebresib, or combined 100 nM C16 and 2.5 nM mivebresib, and RNA isolated by Direct-zol RNA MiniPrep Kit (Zymo Research) with on-column DNAse-treatment. For RNA-seq in MV4;11 NT and RPL22 KO cells, cultures were treated for 48 hr with either 0.1% DMSO or 100 nM C16 before RNA isolation as described above for WINi/BETi RNA-seq. For all RNA-seq experiments, RNA was submitted to the Vanderbilt Technologies for Advanced Genomics (VANTAGE) core facility for library preparation with rRNA-depletion using standard Illumina protocols and sequencing on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000.

### RNA-seq data analysis

Adapters were trimmed from RNA-seq reads using cutadapt (Martin, 2011) and reads aligned to the hg19 genome using STAR (Dobin et al., 2013). Gene expression was quantified using featureCounts (Liao et al., 2014) and differential analysis performed using DESeq2 (Love et al., 2014) which calculates p-values through the Wald test and adjusts p-values by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to calculate FDR. Changes in levels of alternative splicing events were quantified using rMATS, which calculates changes in exon inclusion levels (∆ψ), and p-values through a likelihood-ratio test. Genes with significantly altered transcript levels are those with FDR < 0.05. Significant changes in alternative splicing events are those with FDR < 0.05 and ∆ψ > 5%.

### Generation of Cas9-expressing MV4;11 cells

To generate Cas9 expression lentivirus, HEK293T cells were transfected with the viral transfer plasmid lentiCas9-Blast (Sanjana et al., 2014) (gift from Feng Zhang; Addgene plasmid # 52962), the viral packaging plasmid psPAX2 (gift from Didier Trono; Addgene plasmid # 12260), and the viral envelope plasmid pMD2.G (gift from Didier Trono; Addgene plasmid # 12259) using Lipofectamine 3000 Transfection Reagent (Invitrogen). After 48 hr, virus-containing media was collected and used to transduce MV4;11 cells by spinfection (2 hr; 1000 × g; RT; 8 µg/mL hexadimethrine bromide). Following spinfection, virus-containing media was replaced with fresh media and cells allowed to recover for 48 hr before selection with 10 µg/mL blasticidin (Research Products International). A clonal MV4;11 Cas9 cell line was established by serial dilution of the population and screening for retention of WINi sensitivity.

### Tier 1 CRISPR screen

Tier 1 CRISPR screens were performed essentially as described (Joung et al., 2017). Briefly, the Human GeCKOv2 CRISPR Knockout Pooled Library (A+B) in the lentiGuide-Puro vector backbone (gift from Feng Zhang; Addgene plasmid # 1000000048) was amplified and purified as directed by Addgene. Lentiviral particles were generated by transfecting HEK293T cells with the GeCKOv2 CRISPR Knockout Pooled Plasmid Library, psPAX2 (gift from Didier Trono; Addgene plasmid # 12260), and pMD2.G (gift from Didier Trono; Addgene plasmid # 12259) using Lipofectamine 3000 Transfection Reagent (Invitrogen). After 48 hr, viral media was collected, aliquoted, and stored at –80°C. In duplicate, clonal Cas9-expressing MV4;11 cells were transduced by spinfection (2 hr; 1000 × g; RT; 8 µg/mL hexadimethrine bromide) with a volume of virus-containing media sufficient to infect 30% of cells and at a scale to generate >200 transduced cells per sgRNA in the library. Cells recovered in fresh media overnight, were split 1:2, and selected with 1 µg/mL puromycin for 48 hr to generate the MV4;11 Cas9+GeCKOv2 population.

MV4;11 Cas9 and MV4;11 Cas9+GeCKOv2 cells were treated with either 0.1% DMSO or 2 µM C6, replenished every 3 d with fresh media and C6, and counted daily by trypan blue exclusion. DMSO-treated populations were grown until cultures reached >8 × 105 cells/mL to verify C6-treatment efficacy. C6-treated MV4;11 Cas9+GeCKOv2 populations were maintained below 8 × 105 cells/mL and grown until a resistant population emerged relative to C6-treated MV4;11 Cas9 cells. Genomic DNA was isolated from MV4;11 Cas9+GeCKOv2 cells collected before and following sustained C6 treatment using the Quick-gDNA MidiPrep Kit (Zymo Research) as per the manufacturer’s directions. Sequencing libraries were generated by amplifying sgRNA sequences from genomic DNA using bar-coded Illumina-compatible adapter-containing primers and NEBNext High-Fidelity 2× PCR Master Mix (New England BioLabs). PCR products were pooled and purified with a ZymoSpin V column with Reservoir (Zymo Research). Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 500 in the Vanderbilt Technologies for Advanced Genomics (VANTAGE) core facility.

### Cloning targeted sgRNA library for second-tier screen

The tier 2 sgRNA plasmid library was generated as previously described with some modifications (Joung et al., 2017). Briefly, sgRNA sequences against a curated collection of genes and 200 non-targeting control sgRNA sequences were extracted from the Brunello sgRNA Library (Doench et al., 2016). For genes of interest not included in the Brunello library, four sgRNAs targeting each gene were designed with the CHOPCHOP sgRNA design tool (Labun et al., 2019). sgRNA sequences were appended with 5′ and 3′ flanking sequences and synthesized as an Oligo Pool (Figure 4—source data 2; Twist Bioscience) followed by PCR amplification using NEBNext HiFidelity 2× Master Mix (New England BioLabs) with Fwd primer (GTAACTTGAAAGTATTTCGATTTCTTGGCTTTATATATCTTGTGGAAAGGACGAAACACC) and KO Rev primer (ACTTTTTCAAGTTGATAACGGACTAGCCTTATTTTAACTTGCTATTTCTAGCTCTAAAAC). PCR amplicons were subjected to agarose gel size selection using the NucleoSpin Gel and PCR Clean-up Kit (Macherey-Nagel). Amplicons were cloned into BsmBIv2-digested (New England BioLabs) lentiGuide-PURO plasmid (gift from Feng Zhang; Addgene plasmid # 52963) via Gibson Assembly (New England BioLabs). Gibson Assembly products were precipitated with isopropanol and electroporated into Endura ElectroCompetent Escherichia coli (Lexogen). Amplified plasmids were isolated from E. coli using the Nucleobond Xtra Maxi EF Kit (Macherey-Nagel) and adequate representation of sgRNAs in the library was verified by next-generation sequencing and analysis with the Python script count_spacers.py (Joung et al., 2017).

### Tier 2 CRISPR screen

Tier 2 sgRNA Library lentiviral particles were generated and MV4;11 Cas9 cells transduced as described above for the tier 1 screen at a scale to achieve >500 cells per sgRNA in the library. MV4;11 Cas9+Targeted sgRNA Library populations were treated with either 0.1% DMSO, 2 µM C6, or 100 nM C16 for 15 d. Cultures were maintained below 8 × 105 cells/mL and cultures replenished every 3 d with media and fresh DMSO, C6, or C16. Genomic DNA was isolated, and Illumina-compatible next-generation sequencing libraries generated as described above for the tier 1 screen. Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 in the Vanderbilt Technologies for Advanced Genomics (VANTAGE) core facility.

### CRISPR screen data analysis

Adapters were trimmed from reads using cutadapt (Martin, 2011). Generation of sgRNA count tables and determination of significant gene-level alterations in sgRNA representation were performed using MAGeCK (Li et al., 2014), which utilizes a negative binomial model to determine p-values of sgRNA changes and ranks sgRNAs by significance. Gene-level alterations and p-values were calculated from the ranked list of sgRNAs using the modified robust ranking aggregation (α-RRA) algorithm and FDR values calculated by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Tier 1 screen analysis compared populations before and after C6 treatment. Tier 2 screen analysis compared DMSO-treated populations to C6- or C16-treated populations. Significantly enriched or depleted genes were those with FDR <0.05.

### Cell viability assays

Opaque 384-well plates were seeded with 250 cells per well in 25 µL media supplemented with either 0.1% DMSO or a threefold dilution series of C6 or C16, all in technical quadruplicate wells. Cells were grown for 72 hr before equilibrating to RT and addition of 12.5 µL CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Assay reagent (Promega). At RT and protected from light, plates were rocked for 5 min, incubated for 20 min, and luminescence measured on a GloMax Explorer Multimode Microplate Reader (Promega). To calculate relative cell viability, mean fluorescence from quadruplicate treatment wells was divided by mean fluorescence from quadruplicate DMSO wells. Dose–response curves, GI50 concentrations, and standard error values were calculated from at least three biological replicates with the R package drc (Ritz et al., 2015).

### Synergy assays

Opaque 384-well plates were seeded with 250 cells per well in 25 µL media supplemented with either 0.2% DMSO, a threefold dilution series of either C16 or compound 2, or a combination of threefold dilutions of both C16 and compound 2 covering a 7 × 7 dose matrix, all in quadruplicate wells. Compound 2 consisted of either nutlin-3a (Cayman Chemical Company), rapamycin (MedChem Express), pinometostat (Cayman Chemical Company), harmine (Sigma-Aldrich), mivebresib (Cayman Chemical Company), venetoclax (Cayman Chemical Company), etoposide (Cayman Chemical Company), olaparib (Cayman Chemical Company), VE-821 (Cayman Chemical Company), pemrametostat (Selleck Chemicals), or alvespimycin (Cayman Chemical Company). Following 72 hr, plates were equilibrated to room temperature and 12.5 µL CellTiter-Glo Cell Viability Assay (Promega) reagent added to each well. While protected from light, plates were rocked for 5 min, incubated for 20 min, and luminescence measured on a GloMax Explorer Multimode Microplate Reader (Promega).

### Synergy assay data analysis

Technical replicate wells were averaged and resulting means used to calculate relative cell viability by dividing drug treatment by DMSO treatment. Mean δ-scores and standard deviations were calculated from three biological replicates via SynergyFinder Plus (Zheng et al., 2022) using the ZIP model (Yadav et al., 2015). ZIP δ-scores represent the percent of growth inhibition beyond that expected if the agents do not potentiate one another. δ-scores greater than zero are synergistic, δ-scores of zero are additive, and δ-scores less than zero are antagonistic. Statistical significances of peak synergistic and antagonistic δ-scores were calculated by one-sample t-tests using the tsum.test function from the R package PASWR. Significant synergy and antagonism δ-scores were those with p<0.05.

### Quantitative proteomics

In quadruplicate, MV4;11 cells were seeded at 2 × 105 cells/mL and treated with 0.1% DMSO or 250 nM C16 for either 24 or 72 hr. Cells were collected by centrifugation and washed three times with ice-cold 1× PBS before lysis on ice in SDS Lysis Buffer (5% SDS; 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate). Chromatin was sheared by brief sonication at 25% on ice and insoluble material cleared by centrifugation. Soluble proteins were quantified by Pierce BCA Protein Assay (Thermo Scientific). Of note, protein was isolated from equivalent cell numbers at 24 hr as changes in proliferation are not observed until beyond 24 hr WINi treatment in MV4;11 cells. At 24 hr, DMSO-treated cultures yielded 344.75 ± 21.7 µg total soluble protein and C16-treated cultures yielded 366.50 ± 15.8 µg total soluble protein (mean ± SEM).

Protein samples for LC-MS/MS analyses were prepared by S-Trap (ProtiFi) digestion. Protein samples (50 µg) were reduced with DTT (MilliporeSigma) at a final concentration of 20 mM at 95°C for 10 min and alkylated with iodoacetamide (MilliporeSigma) at a final concentration of 40 mM at RT for 30 min in the dark. Aqueous phosphoric acid (Fisher Scientific) was added to the samples at a final concentration of 1.2% followed by 90% methanol containing 100 mM TEAB at 6.6 times the volume of the sample. The samples were loaded on the S-Trap micro columns and centrifuged at 4000 × g until all the volume was passed through the column. The columns were washed four times with 150 µL 90% methanol containing 100 mM TEAB, pH 7.1. Proteins were digested with trypsin gold (Promega) at 1:50 enzyme to protein ratio in 50 mM TEAB, pH 8.0, for 1 hr at 47°C. Peptides were eluted by serial addition of 40 µL each of 50 mM TEAB, 0.2% formic acid, and 35 µL of 0.2% formic acid in 50% acetonitrile. Eluted peptides were dried in a speed-vac concentrator, resuspended in aqueous 0.1% formic acid, and analyzed by LC-coupled tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS).

An analytical column (360 µm O.D. × 100 µm I.D.) was packed with 25 cm of C18 reverse-phase material (Jupiter, 3 µm beads, 300 Å; Phenomenex) directly into a laser-pulled emitter tip. Peptides were loaded on the reverse phase column using a Dionex Ultimate 3000 nanoLC and autosampler. The mobile phase solvents consisted of 0.1% formic acid, 99.9% water (solvent A) and 0.1% formic acid, 99.9% acetonitrile (solvent B). Peptides were gradient eluted at a flow rate of 350 nL/min using a 120 min gradient. The gradient consisted of the following: 1–100 min, 2–38% B; 100–108 min, 38–90% B; 108–110 min, 90% B; 110–111 min, 90–2% B; 111–120 min (column re-equilibration), 2% B. Upon gradient elution, peptides were analyzed using a data-dependent method on an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific), equipped with a nanoelectrospray ionization source. The instrument method consisted of MS1 using an MS AGC target value of 3 × 106, followed by up to 15 MS/MS scans of the most abundant ions detected in the preceding MS scan. The intensity threshold for triggering data-dependent scans was set to 1 × 104, the MS2 AGC target was set to 1 × 105, dynamic exclusion was set to 20 s, and HCD collision energy was set to 30 nce.

### Quantitative proteomics data analysis

For identification of peptides, LC-MS/MS data were searched with Maxquant, version 2.0.1.0 (Cox and Mann, 2008). MS/MS spectra were searched with the Andromeda search engine (Cox et al., 2011) against a human database created from the UniprotKB protein database (Bateman et al., 2021) and the default Maxquant contaminants. Default parameters were used for Maxquant, with the addition of selecting LFQ and match between runs as a global parameter. Maxquant parameters included first and main search mass tolerances of 20 ppm and 4.5 ppm, respectively. Variable modifications included methionine oxidation and N-terminal acetylation, and carbamidomethyl cysteine was selected as a fixed modification. A maximum of two missed cleavages was allowed. The false discovery rate (FDR) was set to 0.01 for peptide and protein identifications. Label-free quantitative (LFQ) analysis of identified proteins was performed with the MSstats R package (Choi et al., 2014), version 4.0.1, using default parameters, which include the following: equalize medians for the normalization method, log2 transformation, Tukey’s median polish as the summary method, and model-based imputation. Protein fold changes were considered as significant with adjusted p-values ≤0.05.

Building on previous work from the Tansey lab, here Howard et al. characterize transcriptional and translational changes upon WIN site inhibition of WDR5 in MLL-rearranged cancer cells. They first analyze whether C16, a newer generation compound, has the same cellular effects as C6, an early generation compound. Both compounds reduce the expression of WDR5-bound RPGs in addition to the unbound RPG RPL22L1. They then investigate differential translation by ribo-seq and observe that WIN site inhibition reduces the translational RPGs and other proteins related to biomass accumulation (spliceosome, proteasome, mitochondrial ribosome). Unexpectedly, most differentially abundant proteins seem to be upregulated 24 h after C6 (see below). A genetic screen showed that loss of p53 rescues the effect of C6 and C16 and helped the authors to identify pathways that can be targeted by compounds together with WIN site inhibitors in a synergistic way. Finally, the authors elucidated the underlying mechanisms and analyzed the functional relevance of the RPL22, RPL22L1, p53 and MDM4 axis.

Comments on revised version:

The authors have answered my points satisfactorily and the manuscript has become clearer and more meaningful as a result. In particular, the measurement of global translation rate is important and validates the upregulation of a number of proteins following WDR5 inhibitor treatment.

Treatment of MLL-rearranged leukemia cells with high-affinity WINi (C16) decreases the expression of genes encoding most ribosomal proteins and other proteins required for translation. Notably, although these targets are enriched for WDR5-ChIP-seq peaks, such peaks are not universally present in the target genes. High concordance was founded between the alterations in gene expression due to C16 treatment and the changes resulting from treatment with an earlier, lower affinity WINi (C6). Besides protein synthesis, genes involved in DNA replication or MYC responses are downregulated, while p53 targets and apoptosis genes are upregulated. Ribosome profiling reveals a global decrease in translational efficiency due to WINi with overall ribosome occupancies of mRNAs ~50% of control samples. The magnitude in the decrements of translation for most individual mRNAs exceeds the respective changes in mRNA levels genome-wide. From these results and other considerations, the authors hypothesize that WINi results in ribosome depletion. Quantitative mass spec documents the decrement in ribosomal proteins following WINi treatment along with increases in p53 targets and proteins involved in apoptosis occurring over 3 days. Notably RPL22L1 is essentially completely lost upon WINi treatment. The investigators next conduct a CRISPR screen to find moderators and cooperators with WINi. They identify components of p53 and DNA repair pathways as mediators of WINi inflicted cell death (so gRNAs against these genes permit cell survival). Next, WINi are tested in combination with a variety of other agents to explore synergistic killing to improve their expected therapeutic efficacy. The authors document loss of the p53 antagonist MDM4 (in combination with splicing alterations of RPL22L1), an observation that supports the notion that WINi killing is p53-mediated.

This is a scientifically very strong and well-written manuscript that applies a variety of state-of-the art molecular approaches to interrogate the role of the WDR5 interaction site and WINi. They reveal that the effects of WINi seem to be focused on the overall synthesis of protein components of the translation apparatus, especially ribosomal proteins-even those that do not bind WDR5 by ChIP (a question left unanswered is how such the WDR5-less genes are nevertheless WINi targeted). They convincingly show that disruption of the synthesis of these proteins occurs upon activation of p53 dependent apoptosis, likely driven by unbalanced ribosomal protein synthesis leading to MDM2 inhibition. This apoptosis is subsequently followed, as expected by ɣH2AX-activation. Pathways of possible WINi resistance and synergies with other anti-neoplastic approaches are explored. These experiments are all well-executed and strongly invite more extensive pre-clinical and translational studies of WINi in animal studies. The studies also may anticipate the use of WINi as probes of nucleolar function and ribosome synthesis though this was not really explored in the current manuscript. The current version of the manuscript documents ribosomal stress revealed by leakage of NPM1 into the nucleoplasm while nucleolar integrity is preserved. A progressive loss of rRNA synthesis occurs upon drug treatment that is presumably secondary to the decrement in ribosomal protein production.

results.result: C16 is a more potent WDR5 WIN site inhibitor than C6, with ~20-fold greater potency in inhibiting MLLr leukemia cell lines. Both compounds bind the WIN site of WDR5, with C16 having a Kd < 20 pM compared to C6's Kd = 100 pM. The difference in affinity is attributed to C16's bicyclic dihydroisoquinolinone core that locks it into a favorable binding conformation.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C40 are well-supported by crystal structure data (Figure 1B, C), binding affinity measurements from cited work (Tian et al., 2020; Aho et al., 2019a), and cell viability assays showing ~20-fold difference in GI50 values (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C). The structural basis for the affinity difference is demonstrated through crystallographic analysis.

results.result: C6 and C16 induce similar transcriptional responses in MLLr cells, with thousands of gene expression changes that are predominantly less than twofold in magnitude. Both compounds suppress WDR5-bound genes and induce p53 target genes, with >80% overlap in affected transcripts. The transcriptional effects on RPG expression are almost entirely confined to WDR5-bound RPGs, with the notable exception of RPL22L1, which is strongly suppressed despite not being a direct WDR5 target.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C50 are supported by comprehensive RNA-seq data (Figure 1E-J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) showing similar transcriptional profiles between C6 and C16, GSEA analysis demonstrating enrichment of WDR5-bound genes among suppressed genes (Figure 1H), and enrichment analysis showing induction of p53 pathways (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B). The RPL22L1 exception is consistently observed across multiple cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).

results.result: WINi induce a progressive, time-dependent decrease in protein synthesis capacity, with no significant effect at 24 hr but reaching ~40% reduction by 96 hr. Ribo-seq analysis reveals that WINi cause widespread translational inhibition affecting ~4,500-5,900 transcripts, with changes generally less than twofold in magnitude. The translational effects are largely independent of basal translation efficiencies, though mRNAs with 5'TOP motifs show less decrease in translation efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C61 are supported by OPP labeling data showing time-dependent decline in protein synthesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B), comprehensive Ribo-seq data demonstrating widespread but modest decreases in translation efficiency (Figure 2A-E), and analysis showing that highly translated transcripts are more affected (Figure 2E). The 5'TOP motif observation is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E with appropriate citation to Philippe et al., 2020.

results.result: WINi cause translational suppression that extends beyond transcriptional effects, affecting more genes in categories linked to MYC, E2F, mTORC1 signaling, and the G2M checkpoint. The translational effects include genes connected to the proteasome, spliceosome, mRNA surveillance, and translation machinery, including an expanded cohort of RPG transcripts beyond those directly bound by WDR5. This represents a widespread reduction in the ability of MLLr cells to efficiently translate mRNAs connected to protein synthesis and homeostasis.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C72 are supported by comparative analysis of RNA-seq and Ribo-seq data showing that translational effects encompass more genes than transcriptional effects (Figure 2F-H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F-G), enrichment analysis demonstrating affected biological categories (Figure 2G, Figure 2—source data 2), and data showing that translational effects on RPGs extend beyond WDR5-bound genes (Figure 2H). The PRMT5 substrate analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F) and codon usage analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I) provide additional mechanistic support.

results.result: WINi deplete the entire inventory of cytosolic ribosomes, not just those encoded by WDR5-bound genes. LFQMS analysis tracking ~3,200 proteins shows progressive decline in ribosomal protein levels, with most changes less than twofold in magnitude. By 72 hr, almost all ribosomal subunits are in deficit regardless of WDR5 binding status. RPL22L1 is the most strongly suppressed protein at 72 hr, with levels reduced by an order of magnitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C88 are supported by comprehensive LFQMS data (Figure 3A-G) showing time-dependent depletion of ribosomal proteins, enrichment analysis demonstrating significant enrichment of ribosome-linked proteins among those reduced in abundance (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), and specific data showing that both WDR5-bound and non-bound RPGs are affected at the protein level (Figure 3G). The progressive nature of the response is well-documented across the two timepoints.

results.result: WINi trigger nucleolar stress responses, as evidenced by progressive decline in rRNA expression (measured by metabolic labeling with AzCyd) and decreased nucleolar enrichment of NPM1 at 72 hr. However, γ-H2AX is only detected in morphologically apoptotic cells, not in non-apoptotic cells, indicating that widespread DNA damage induction is not a specific consequence of WINi action, unlike some rRNA inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 are supported by metabolic labeling data showing progressive decline in rRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), immunofluorescence data demonstrating NPM1 redistribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), and γ-H2AX staining showing DNA damage only in apoptotic cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A). The conclusion about nucleolar stress is appropriately supported by the NPM1 data and citation to Aho et al., 2019a, while the distinction from rRNA inhibitors is supported by the γ-H2AX data and citation to Rogakou et al., 2000.

results.result: A two-tier CRISPR screen identified genes that modulate the response to WINi in MLLr cells. TP53 is the most highly enriched gene, followed by RPL22. The tier 2 screen revealed that C6 and C16 have very similar response profiles, with 57 common genes enriched in four overlapping categories: p53 signaling, apoptosis, DNA damage response, and histone modifications. BRD3 emerged as a conspicuous sensitizing gene in the histone modification category.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C107 are supported by comprehensive CRISPR screen data (Figure 4B-E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-I) showing enrichment of TP53 and RPL22, high concordance between C6 and C16 responses (Figure 4C-D), GO enrichment analysis identifying the four major categories (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), and specific data on BRD3 and SPOP (Figure 4E). The miRNA network analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) and p53 effector data provide additional support for the importance of p53 signaling.

results.result: C16 shows synergy with multiple agents in MLLr cells, including mivebresib, pemrametostat, pinometostat, etoposide, harmine, and venetoclax in MV4;11 cells. Four agents (mivebresib, pemrametostat, pinometostat, and venetoclax) show particularly strong synergy (peak δ-scores > 10) at doses consistent with on-target activity, and all four are synergistic with C16 in both MV4;11 and MOLM13 cells. Rapamycin shows potent antagonism with C16.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C113 are supported by comprehensive synergy assay data using the ZIP model (Figure 5A-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1-2), showing peak δ-scores for various combinations and demonstrating reproducibility across two MLLr cell lines. The data are appropriately analyzed with statistical thresholds and dose-response matrices are provided. The antagonism with rapamycin is clearly demonstrated with a peak δ-score of -16.

results.result: The synergy between C16 and mivebresib is apparent at the transcript level, with >6,200 gene expression changes in the combination treatment compared to <1,800 for C16 and 2,700 for mivebresib alone. The two agents induce very distinct transcriptional profiles with <200 shared gene expression changes in each direction. The combination dysregulates similar categories of genes as each agent alone but with substantially more genes in each category, consistent with synergy resulting from alterations in distinct but complementary sets of genes that augment p53 induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C118 are supported by RNA-seq data from combination treatment (Figure 5E-H, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-B) showing additive effects on RPG expression, distinct transcriptional profiles for each agent, and enhanced effects in the combination. The enrichment analysis (Figure 5—source data 3) demonstrates that similar categories are affected but with more genes in the combination. However, the mechanistic interpretation (C118) is appropriately qualified as requiring further investigation.

results.result: WINi cause only a slight increase in p53 protein levels but promote accumulation of MDM4 transcripts in which exon 6 is skipped, leading to reduced MDM4 protein expression. WINi also lead to depletion of transcripts encoding the RPL22L1a isoform that is incorporated into ribosomes, while the splicing-relevant RPL22L1b isoform is insensitive to WINi. Alternative splicing analysis reveals ~1,000 differentially spliced mRNAs for each WINi.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C129 are supported by western blot data showing modest p53 induction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), alternative splicing analysis using rMATS (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), Sashimi plots demonstrating MDM4 exon 6 skipping (Figure 6B) and RPL22L1 isoform changes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), and validation by semi-quantitative and quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F-G). The citations to prior work (Ghandi et al., 2019; Rallapalli et al., 1999; Francoz et al., 2006; Bieging-Rolett et al., 2020; Muys et al., 2021; Larionova et al., 2022) appropriately support the mechanistic context.

results.result: RPL22 knockout decreases the sensitivity of MV4;11 and MOLM13 cells to C16 by 3- to 5-fold and attenuates p53 induction, while having no effect on p53-null K562 cells. RPL22 disruption does not impact the effect of WINi on WDR5-bound RPGs but blocks the effects on RPL22L1 and ZMAT3 expression and impairs induction of p53 signaling genes. RPL22 is needed for a majority of the characteristic responses of MLLr cells to WINi, including p53 activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C137 are supported by cell viability assays showing reduced sensitivity in RPL22 KO cells (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), western blot data showing attenuated p53 induction (Figure 6D), and comprehensive RNA-seq analysis (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-H) demonstrating that RPL22 loss blocks specific aspects of the WINi response while not affecting WDR5-bound RPG suppression. The differential effect on K562 cells provides important specificity control.

results.result: RPL22 disruption promotes exon 6 retention in MDM4 and induces RPL22L1a expression in the absence of WINi. In the presence of C16, RPL22 disruption mitigates MDM4 exon 6 skipping and largely blocks suppression of the RPL22L1a-encoding mRNA isoform. These changes manifest at the protein level, with C16 suppressing both MDM4 and RPL22L1 protein expression, and RPL22 loss blocking the majority of C16's ability to reduce MDM4 and RPL22L1 proteins and to induce p21. Splicing-driven suppression of MDM4 is an important mechanism through which WINi activate p53 in MLLr cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C146 are supported by alternative splicing analysis showing the effects of RPL22 KO on MDM4 and RPL22L1 splicing (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 3B-C), western blot data demonstrating protein-level changes (Figure 6G), and the integration of these findings with prior work (Ghandi et al., 2019). The conclusion about splicing-driven MDM4 suppression as a mechanism of p53 activation is well-supported by the convergence of splicing, protein expression, and functional data.

results.result: The primary targets of WINi are proposed to be the ~40 RPGs bound by WDR5 in all cell types, which are rapidly transcriptionally suppressed and whose function depends on WDR5 recruiting MYC. Ribosomal protein depletion is driven partly by decreased translation of ribosomal mRNAs, with effects capping at ~30% decrease by 72 hr. This corresponds to a loss of up to 3 million ribosomes per cell and results in reduced translational efficiencies of about half of all actively translated mRNAs. WINi also trigger progressive decline in rRNA expression and promote nucleolar stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C157 are supported by integration of data from multiple experiments (RNA-seq, Ribo-seq, LFQMS, metabolic labeling, immunofluorescence) and appropriate citations to prior work (Aho et al., 2019a; Bryan et al., 2020; Florian et al., 2022; Thomas et al., 2019; Ahmadi et al., 2021; Siladi et al., 2022; Shore and Albert, 2022; Dörner et al., 2023). The proposed mechanism is appropriately qualified as a model and the quantitative estimates (30% decrease, 3 million ribosomes) are supported by cited work.

results.result: Activation of p53 is a major point of convergence between WDR5 and rRNA inhibitors. While rRNA inhibitors are thought to activate p53 by generating excess ribosomal proteins that inactivate MDM2, WINi activate p53 through a second route involving alternative splicing of MDM4 mRNA to promote exon 6 skipping, driving down MDM4 protein levels. Because MDM4 inhibits p53 via proteolysis-independent mechanisms, this explains how WINi can induce a robust p53 target gene signature without frank induction of p53 protein, pointing to a dominant role of the MDM4-p53 axis in mediating the response to WIN site blockade.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C165 are supported by the integration of data showing modest p53 protein induction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), robust p53 target gene induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B), MDM4 splicing changes (Figure 6B), and the functional importance of this pathway demonstrated by RPL22 KO experiments (Figure 6C-G). The mechanistic interpretation is appropriately supported by citations to prior work on MDM4 function (Francoz et al., 2006) and rRNA inhibitor mechanisms (Pfister, 2019). The conclusion about the dominant role of the MDM4-p53 axis is well-supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: The mechanism through which WINi inactivate MDM4 may involve the balance of RPL22L1 and ZMAT3, which are oppositely regulated in response to WIN site inhibition. ZMAT3 is induced by p53 activation and promotes MDM4 exon 6 skipping, while RPL22L1 promotes exon 6 inclusion. However, the isoform of RPL22L1 suppressed by WINi (RPL22L1a) is linked to ribosome function rather than splicing in glioblastoma cells, while the splicing-relevant RPL22L1b isoform is resistant to WINi, creating a paradox regarding the mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C173 represent speculative mechanistic proposals that are appropriately qualified as possibilities and alternatives. While the data on ZMAT3 induction and RPL22L1 suppression are supported (with appropriate citations to Bieging-Rolett et al., 2020 and Larionova et al., 2022), the authors acknowledge the paradox regarding RPL22L1 isoforms and present alternative explanations without definitive resolution. The uncertainty is appropriately acknowledged in the text, and the claims are presented as hypotheses requiring further investigation rather than established facts.

results.result: Loss of RPL22 causes induction of RPL22L1 and promotes inclusion of exon 6 in MDM4, as inferred from CCLE studies and demonstrated experimentally. RPL22 itself does not appear to play a role in the response to WINi in unperturbed MLLr cells; rather, its recovery as a resistance gene in the CRISPR screen is tied to its ability to suppress RPL22L1 expression and the ectopic effect of its deletion on preventing WINi-induced RPL22L1a decline. RPL22 status is likely highly relevant for patient selection, as RPL22 is frequently inactivated or deleted in 7% of CCLE lines and primary cancers, with a strong tendency for wild-type p53 retention. Cancers with RPL22 mutations/deletions or RPL22L1 overexpression would not be expected to robustly respond to WINi.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C181 are supported by experimental data from RPL22 KO experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B-C, Figure 6G) demonstrating the effects on RPL22L1 and MDM4, appropriate citations to CCLE studies (Ghandi et al., 2019; Cao et al., 2017; Kandoth et al., 2013; Goudarzi and Lindström, 2016), and citation to O'Leary et al., 2013 for RPL22's ability to suppress RPL22L1. The conclusion about patient selection criteria is a reasonable inference from the data, though it would require clinical validation.

results.result: Although p53 is important for WINi action in MLLr cells, there are likely other stress response mechanisms that mediate cellular inhibition. Four resistance genes identified in the CRISPR screen (UBA6, BIRC6, KCMF1, and UBR4) encode members of the BIRC6 ubiquitin-ligase complex, which prevents aberrant activation of the integrated stress response (ISR). While there is no indication that the ISR is activated by WINi (ATF4 is suppressed), the finding that loss of all four BIRC6 complex members blunts the response to WINi implies that ISR activation can be a mechanism through which cells evade the full impact of these agents.
results.evaluation: Claims C182-C187 are supported by the CRISPR screen data identifying the four BIRC6 complex members as resistance genes, appropriate citations to prior work on p53-independent nucleolar stress responses (Boglev et al., 2013; Pfister et al., 2015; Jayaraman et al., 2017) and the BIRC6 complex (Cervia et al., 2023), and RNA-seq/Ribo-seq data showing ATF4 suppression. The inference about ISR activation as a potential evasion mechanism is appropriately qualified and supported by the genetic data.

results.result: Future single-agent WINi treatment paradigms are likely to encounter resistance through activation of protective responses or mutations in resistance genes. The combination with mivebresib is rationalized by identification of BRD3 as a sensitizing gene and likely results from C16 and mivebresib inhibiting distinct sets of genes connected to translation, enhancing p53 induction. This combination would be expected to be effective in other wild-type p53 cancer settings where WINi are active, such as neuroblastoma and rhabdoid tumors.
results.evaluation: Claims C188-C190 are supported by the CRISPR screen data identifying resistance genes (Figure 4), synergy data demonstrating strong synergy between C16 and mivebresib (Figure 5A-D), RNA-seq data showing distinct but complementary effects on translation-related genes (Figure 5E-H), and appropriate citations to prior work showing WINi activity in neuroblastoma and rhabdoid tumors (Bryan et al., 2020; Florian et al., 2022). However, C188 and C190 are appropriately qualified as expectations/predictions rather than established facts, as they would require clinical validation.

results.result: WDR5 is a highly conserved, multifunctional nuclear protein that rose to prominence as a component of H3K4 methyltransferase complexes but also acts outside these complexes to facilitate mitotic spindle integrity, gene bookmarking, and transcription of ribosomal protein genes via MYC recruitment. WDR5 is frequently overexpressed in cancer, correlating with aggressive disease and poor clinical outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are background claims supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Guarnaccia and Tansey, 2018; Ali et al., 2017; Oh et al., 2020; Bryan et al., 2020; Thomas et al., 2019). These are well-established facts in the field that provide context for the current study.

results.result: WDR5 is an auspicious target for inhibition in multiple malignancies including MLLr leukemias, MYC-driven cancers, and various other cancer types. Most drug discovery efforts have focused on small-molecule inhibition of key binding sites, particularly the WIN site, with multiple WINi described including orally bioavailable compounds with in vivo antitumor activity. However, controversy remains regarding the mechanism of action of WINi, even in MLLr leukemias.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C21 are background claims supported by extensive citations to prior work documenting WDR5 as a therapeutic target in various cancers, the development of WIN site inhibitors, and the controversy regarding their mechanism of action (Weissmiller et al., 2024). These provide appropriate context for the current study. C20 is appropriately qualified as a likelihood rather than a certainty.

results.result: MLLr leukemias are defined by translocation of MLL1, and early models proposed that these leukemias depend on wild-type MLL1 to support MLL1-fusion oncoproteins through WIN site interaction with WDR5. Early peptidomimetic WINi were reported to suppress H3K4 methylation at MLL1-fusion target genes. However, wild-type MLL1 was subsequently shown to be dispensable for transformation, and picomolar small-molecule WINi act without inducing significant changes in HOXA gene expression or H3K4 methylation levels. Instead, WINi displace WDR5 from chromatin and suppress transcription of ~50 genes connected to protein synthesis, provoke nucleolar stress, and induce p53-dependent cell death.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C30 are background claims supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Guarnaccia and Tansey, 2018; Thiel et al., 2010; Alicea-Velázquez et al., 2016; Cao et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2017; Aho et al., 2019a). These provide important historical context for the evolution of understanding of WINi mechanism of action and set up the rationale for the current study.

results.result: Inhibition of rRNA production or processing is a feature of both existing chemotherapies and newer targeted RNA polymerase I inhibitors. These agents are generally thought to disrupt ribosome stoichiometry, leading to excess ribosomal proteins that inactivate MDM2 to induce p53-dependent cell death. A significant point of divergence from rRNA poisons is that WINi are proposed to induce p53 not by promoting excess ribosomal protein accumulation, but by causing a selective imbalance in the ribosome subunit inventory.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 are background claims supported by appropriate citations (Bruno et al., 2017; Drygin et al., 2011; Peltonen et al., 2014; Laham-Karam et al., 2020) that provide context for understanding WINi as a novel type of ribosome-directed therapy. C33 is appropriately qualified as a proposed model rather than an established fact, and the current study's data (showing depletion of the entire ribosome inventory rather than selective imbalance) actually refines this earlier model.

results.result: C16 and C6 are both WIN site inhibitors with similar cellular effects in MLL-rearranged leukemia cells. C16 is ~20 times more potent than C6, with both compounds suppressing WDR5-bound RPGs and inducing similar transcriptional changes including p53 target genes, with the notable exception of RPL22L1 which is suppressed despite not being a direct WDR5 target.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers affirm these findings. Reviewer 1 states 'Both compounds reduce the expression of WDR5-bound RPGs in addition to the unbound RPG RPL22L1' and notes 'High concordance was founded between the alterations in gene expression due to C16 treatment and the changes resulting from treatment with an earlier, lower affinity WINi (C6).' Reviewer 2 confirms the data is 'generally very convincing' and the editor notes the data 'buttresses the authors' conclusions and interpretations quite nicely.'

results.result: WINi induce widespread translational suppression affecting ~4,500-5,900 transcripts with decreased translation efficiency (TE), with effects generally less than twofold. The translational effects extend beyond transcriptional changes and affect genes connected to protein synthesis, spliceosome, proteasome, and translation machinery, including both WDR5-bound and non-WDR5-bound RPGs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly confirms 'WIN site inhibition reduces the translational RPGs and other proteins related to biomass accumulation (spliceosome, proteasome, mitochondrial ribosome)' and notes 'this reduction adds to the transcriptional changes and is not limited to RPGs whose promoters are bound by WDR5.' Reviewer 2 states the ribosome profiling data 'reveals a global decrease in translational efficiency' and the findings are 'convincingly shown.' The editor affirms the data is 'very convincing.'

results.result: WINi cause progressive depletion of ribosomal proteins over time (24-72 hr), with effects becoming more pronounced at later timepoints. By 72 hr, almost all ribosomal subunits are depleted regardless of WDR5 binding status, with RPL22L1 being the most strongly suppressed protein. This is accompanied by progressive decline in rRNA expression and induction of p53 target proteins.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 confirms 'Quantitative proteomics at two time points confirmed the downregulation of RPGs' and notes 'RPL22LA is strongly affected.' Reviewer 2 states 'Quantitative mass spec documents the decrement in ribosomal proteins following WINi treatment along with increases in p53 targets and proteins involved in apoptosis occurring over 3 days.' The measurement of global translation rate was specifically noted by Reviewer 1 as 'important and validates the upregulation of a number of proteins following WDR5 inhibitor treatment.'

results.result: WINi induce nucleolar stress as evidenced by decreased nucleolar enrichment of NPM1 at 72 hr, but do not cause widespread DNA damage induction. γ-H2AX is only detected in morphologically apoptotic cells, not in non-apoptotic cells, distinguishing WINi from some rRNA inhibitors.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly confirms 'The current version of the manuscript documents ribosomal stress revealed by leakage of NPM1 into the nucleoplasm while nucleolar integrity is preserved.' The distinction from rRNA inhibitors regarding DNA damage is accepted without challenge. Reviewer 2 notes 'apoptosis is subsequently followed, as expected by γH2AX-activation' in the context of apoptotic cells.

results.result: CRISPR screens identify TP53 as the most highly enriched resistance gene, with CDKN2A (p14ARF) and RPL22 also highly enriched. The tier 2 screen reveals 57 common genes enriched in four categories: p53 signaling, apoptosis, DNA damage response, and histone modifications, with BRD3 identified as a key sensitizing gene.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'A genetic screen showed that loss of p53 rescues the effect of C6 and C16 and helped the authors to identify pathways that can be targeted by compounds together with WIN site inhibitors in a synergistic way.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'They identify components of p53 and DNA repair pathways as mediators of WINi inflicted cell death (so gRNAs against these genes permit cell survival).' The identification of specific genes and pathways is accepted without challenge by all reviewers.

results.result: C16 shows synergy with multiple agents including mivebresib, pemrametostat, pinometostat, and venetoclax in MLLr cells. The combination with mivebresib is particularly strong and results from distinct but complementary transcriptional effects that enhance p53 induction, with the combination affecting substantially more genes than either agent alone.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes 'Pathways of possible WINi resistance and synergies with other anti-neoplastic approaches are explored. These experiments are all well-executed.' The synergy data and mechanistic interpretation are accepted without specific critique. The editor affirms the overall data is 'very convincing' and supports the conclusions about therapeutic combinations.

results.result: WINi promote alternative splicing changes including skipping of exon 6 in MDM4 and depletion of the RPL22L1a isoform. RPL22 knockout decreases sensitivity to C16 by 3-5 fold in MLLr cells and blocks most characteristic responses including p53 activation, MDM4 suppression, and RPL22L1 reduction, demonstrating that splicing-driven suppression of MDM4 is an important mechanism of p53 activation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'The authors document loss of the p53 antagonist MDM4 (in combination with splicing alterations of RPL22L1), an observation that supports the notion that WINi killing is p53-mediated.' The RPL22 knockout experiments and their effects on the response to WINi are accepted without challenge. Reviewer 1 confirms the authors 'analyzed the functional relevance of the RPL22, RPL22L1, p53 and MDM4 axis' and found the manuscript 'clearer and more meaningful' after revisions.

results.result: The proposed mechanism is that WINi primarily target ~40 WDR5-bound RPGs, leading to ribosomal protein depletion (capped at ~30% decrease) and progressive rRNA decline. This activates p53 through two routes: MDM2 inhibition via excess ribosomal proteins and MDM4 suppression via alternative splicing, with the MDM4-p53 axis playing a dominant role.
results.evaluation: The editor states 'This important article reveals that one of the major roles of the WDR5 WIN site is to promote ribosome synthesis, and that by attacking the WIN site with inhibitors ribosome attrition occurs creating new vulnerabilities that can be therapeutically exploited. This deficiency of ribosomal proteins also provokes the p53 response.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'They convincingly show that disruption of the synthesis of these proteins occurs upon activation of p53 dependent apoptosis, likely driven by unbalanced ribosomal protein synthesis leading to MDM2 inhibition.' The mechanistic model is accepted as well-supported.

results.result: RPL22 status is clinically relevant for patient selection, as RPL22 is frequently inactivated/deleted in cancers (7% of CCLE lines) and unlike other RPGs, RPL22 mutation/deletion is associated with retention of wild-type p53. Cancers with RPL22 mutation/deletion or RPL22L1 overexpression would not be expected to respond robustly to WINi.
results.evaluation: This conclusion follows logically from the accepted RPL22 knockout data and is not challenged by reviewers. Reviewer 2 notes the studies 'strongly invite more extensive pre-clinical and translational studies of WINi in animal studies,' implicitly accepting the clinical relevance of these findings. The patient selection implications are a logical extension of the experimental data that reviewers found convincing.

results.result: The synergy between C16 and BET inhibitors (particularly mivebresib) is rationalized by BRD3 identification in the CRISPR screen and results from inhibition of distinct gene sets connected to translation that enhance p53 induction. This combination is expected to be effective in other wild-type p53 cancers where WINi are active.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states the experiments exploring synergies 'are all well-executed and strongly invite more extensive pre-clinical and translational studies of WINi in animal studies.' The mechanistic rationale for the combination based on the CRISPR screen and transcriptional data is accepted. The extension to other cancer types is a reasonable inference from the mechanism that is not challenged by reviewers.

comparisons.comparison: Strong agreement on proteomics findings (C73-C88). Both confirm time-dependent depletion of ribosomal proteins and enrichment of ribosome-linked proteins. OpenEval provides detailed analysis of WDR5-bound vs non-bound RPGs, while peer review emphasizes validation of global translation rate measurement and RPL22LA effects.

Strong agreement on CRISPR screen results (C94-C107). Both confirm enrichment of TP53 and RPL22, high concordance between C6 and C16, and identification of four major GO categories. Peer review emphasizes the screen's utility for identifying synergistic pathways.

Strong agreement on nucleolar stress findings (C89-C93). Both confirm NPM1 redistribution as evidence of nucleolar stress and distinction from rRNA inhibitors regarding DNA damage. Peer review explicitly notes preserved nucleolar integrity and γH2AX activation in apoptotic cells.

Strong agreement on RNA-seq findings (C41-C50). Both confirm similar transcriptional profiles between C6 and C16, suppression of WDR5-bound RPGs, GSEA enrichment, and p53 pathway induction. Peer review notes high concordance between compounds and finds data 'generally very convincing.'

Partial overlap on structural and binding data (C34-C40 in OpenEval vs C37-C50 in peer review). Both support crystal structure findings and binding affinity differences. OpenEval focuses on structural basis while peer review emphasizes transcriptional effects of both compounds.

Strong agreement on translational effects (C62-C72). Both confirm that translational effects encompass more genes than transcriptional effects and affect multiple biological categories. Peer review explicitly confirms 'global decrease in translational efficiency' and finds data 'convincingly shown.'

Strong agreement on Ribo-seq findings (C51-C61). Both confirm time-dependent decline in protein synthesis and widespread decreases in translation efficiency. Peer review confirms global translation reduction and notes findings are 'convincingly shown.'

Strong agreement on synergy data (C108-C113). Both confirm synergistic interactions using ZIP model and antagonism with rapamycin. Peer review notes experiments are 'all well-executed' and support therapeutic combination strategies.

Strong agreement on combination treatment transcriptional effects (C114-C118). Both confirm additive effects on RPG expression and distinct profiles for each agent. Peer review accepts mechanistic interpretation while OpenEval appropriately qualifies it as requiring further investigation.

Strong agreement on RPL22-mediated splicing effects (C138-C146). Both confirm RPL22 KO effects on MDM4 and RPL22L1 splicing and protein-level changes. Peer review states authors 'document loss of the p53 antagonist MDM4' and accepts splicing-driven mechanism.

Strong agreement on RPL22 KO functional effects (C130-C137). Both confirm reduced sensitivity in RPL22 KO cells, attenuated p53 induction, and selective blocking of WINi response aspects. Peer review accepts RPL22 knockout experiments without challenge.

Strong agreement on alternative splicing findings (C119-C129). Both confirm modest p53 induction, MDM4 exon 6 skipping, and RPL22L1 isoform changes. Peer review accepts the functional relevance of the RPL22-RPL22L1-p53-MDM4 axis.

Strong agreement on integrated mechanistic model (C147-C157). Both support the ribosome attrition model and its connection to p53 activation. Editor explicitly states article 'reveals that one of the major roles of the WDR5 WIN site is to promote ribosome synthesis' and accepts the mechanistic framework.

Strong agreement on MDM4-p53 axis as dominant mechanism (C158-C165). Both confirm modest p53 protein induction leads to robust target gene induction via MDM4 splicing changes. Peer review states findings 'convincingly show' p53-dependent apoptosis driven by unbalanced ribosomal protein synthesis.

Strong agreement on patient selection implications (C174-C181). Both accept that RPL22 status and TP53 status are relevant for patient selection. Peer review implicitly accepts clinical relevance by noting studies 'strongly invite more extensive pre-clinical and translational studies.'

Strong agreement on therapeutic implications (C188-C190). Both support extension to other cancer types and combination strategies. Peer review states synergy experiments 'are all well-executed and strongly invite more extensive pre-clinical and translational studies.'

OpenEval supports claims about BIRC6 complex and ISR activation as resistance mechanisms (C182-C187) based on CRISPR screen data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though these findings are part of the accepted resistance pathway analysis.

OpenEval confirms background claims about WIN site inhibitors and therapeutic targeting (C7-C21) are well-supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation as these provide study context.
